Note::lengths_graphemes¶

Back to Note API Reference

Signature¶

Note Note::lengths_graphemes() const

Measure Every Cell In Grapheme Clusters¶

lengths_graphemes() returns the length of each text cell counted in extended grapheme clusters — “what a reader would call a character.” A base letter and the combining marks that attach to it count as one, so this is the measurement to use for cursor movement, column alignment, and “visible length” limits.

The difference from lengths_chars appears whenever text uses combining marks: "e" followed by U+0301 (combining acute accent) is one grapheme but two code points. Precomposed text ("café" written with a single é code point) counts the same either way.

Segmentation follows the Unicode default grapheme-break algorithm (UAX #29) via the library’s Unicode backend. One known limitation: ZWJ emoji sequences (a family emoji, a flag, a profession emoji) are not joined into a single cluster by the current backend, so they count as several graphemes. When the Unicode backend is unavailable, this method falls back to the code-point count.

Return value¶

An Int64 Note with the receiver’s shape, one native count per cell. An empty cell measures 0; integers() exposes a borrowed contiguous host view.

Example 1: A Combining Mark Counts As One¶

const std::string e_acute = "e\xCC\x81";  // "e" + U+0301
const auto lens =
    pluss::make_note({e_acute, "abc"}).lengths_graphemes();
std::cout << "[";
for (std::size_t i = 0; i < lens.integers().size(); ++i)
  std::cout << (i ? ", " : "") << lens.integers()[i];
std::cout << "]\n";

Output¶

[1, 3]

The decomposed é is one grapheme; "abc" is three.

Example 2: Contrast With lengths_chars¶

const std::string e_acute = "e\xCC\x81";
const auto chars = pluss::make_note({e_acute}).lengths_chars();
std::cout << "[" << chars[0] << "]\n";

Output¶

[2]

Same cell: 2 code points, 1 grapheme.

Example 3: Precomposed Text Counts The Same As Characters¶

const auto lens =
    pluss::make_note({"café", "日本語"}).lengths_graphemes();
std::cout << "[";
for (std::size_t i = 0; i < lens.integers().size(); ++i)
  std::cout << (i ? ", " : "") << lens.integers()[i];
std::cout << "]\n";

Output¶

[4, 3]
